newsitem.title: USA: U.S. CFTC reviews March wheat 'squeeze' penalties.
newsitem.headline: U.S. CFTC reviews March wheat 'squeeze' penalties.

text.p: U.S. regulators, acting on a staff report that alleged inadequate penalties for a March wheat-trading frenzy, said Friday they would review the Chicago Board of Trade's disciplinary actions.

The staff report to the Commodity Futures Trading Commission said traders improperly sold contracts for two minutes after the scheduled expiration of the March wheat contract. Onlookers crowded the wheat pit and roared as prices bounded to a record $7.50 a bushel, a climb of nearly 50 percent in less than three minutes.
Two "local" traders made a combined profit of $587,000 from the sales. They commanded a high price because Bunge Corp needed wheat to meet its obligations. Bunge lost $300,000.

Six participants in the sales were given letters of reprimand from a CBOT disciplinary panel. Louis Dreyfus Corp and subsidiary Term Commodities jointly paid $10,000 because they wrongly sold wheat in a "modified closing call," held a few minutes after the frenzied "expiration" trading, to close out unliquidated positions.

While the staff report suggested the CFTC should direct the Chicago Board of Trade to impose more stringent penalties, the CFTC gave the CBOT and the six participants 30 days to respond to the report. It said the staff would have 30 days after that for rebuttal.
CBOT officials were not immediately available for comment.

CFTC staff said the improper continuation of trading was a serious violation that could undermine confidence in CBOT prices and must be treated gravely. Letters of reprimand to five traders and a Bunge subsidiary "were inadequate...and may not sufficiently deter future conduct," they said.
In addition, the report said, the sanctions against those participants "appear to be inconsistent" with the fine paid by Dreyfus and Term, who said they repsponded to a call for liquidity.

"The (CFTC investigators) believe the fact that firms were fined, while individual exchange members who held customer orders were not, to be disparate treatment of the parties for which the exchange has not provided any justification," the report said.
The CBOT instituted five rules changes to ensure trading ends on time for expiring contracts and to spell out how to set prices during a "modified closing call."
